04 — Portfolio strategies and backtest (100 experiments)¶

In this notebook we compare the strategies of part 2 of the project brief:

Strategy Idea
a) Equally weighted (EW) the same weight in every stock (main benchmark)
b) Markowitz mean-variance maximise return − (λ/2)·variance, with risk aversion λ = 3
c) Global minimum variance (GMV) the portfolio with the lowest possible volatility
d) Max Sharpe the portfolio with the highest expected Sharpe ratio
e) Inverse volatility and Risk parity (ERC) weights inversely proportional to volatility / equal risk contributions
f) Most diversified and Max decorrelation maximise the diversification ratio / minimise the average correlation

There are 8 strategies. We also test a 9th portfolio, the Group pick (23 stocks): the group's own selection of 23 S&P 500 stocks (notebook 01), each equally weighted and rebalanced exactly like the other strategies (see section 3). SPY (the investable S&P 500 ETF) is used as the market benchmark. So 10 portfolios appear in every table and chart of the main backtest, and section 9.5 compares all of them against each other (head-to-head).

Conventions (the same for every strategy)¶

Item Choice
Universe 23 S&P 500 stocks chosen in notebook 01
Data adjusted close prices (Yahoo Finance), daily, 2010-01-04 to 2026-09-18
Returns simple returns for the portfolios (log returns were only used for the stylised facts)
Experiments 100, random seed 2026
Each experiment one contiguous 3-year period (756 trading days) + 12 stocks drawn from the 23 (the Group pick always holds all the eligible stocks: 23, or 22 before TSLA has data)
Split years 1–2 = estimation; year 3 = out-of-sample evaluation (252 days)
Estimation window rolling, 1 year (252 days), using only data from before the rebalancing date
Rebalancing semi-annual (126 trading days); between dates the weights drift with prices
Constraints long-only (weights ≥ 0), fully invested (sum = 1), no leverage
Risk-free rate 3-year Treasury yield (FRED, series DGS3); daily rate = annual rate / 252
Transaction costs 10 bps on the traded value (Σ|Δw|); robustness checks with 0, 25 and 50 bps
Benchmarks EW (main), the Group pick and SPY buy & hold

1. Backtest parameters¶

All the parameters are here at the top, so that it is easy to change them and run everything again.

In [2]:
SEED = 2026                 # random seed -> guarantees that the 100 experiments are always the same
N_EXPERIMENTS = 100         # number of 3-year datasets
N_ASSETS = 12               # number of stocks drawn in each experiment (out of 23)

DAYS_PER_YEAR = 252                     # trading days in one year
DATASET_DAYS = 3 * DAYS_PER_YEAR        # 756 days = 3 years
EVAL_START = 2 * DAYS_PER_YEAR          # day 504: the first 2 years are used for estimation
ESTIMATION_WINDOW = DAYS_PER_YEAR       # rolling 1-year window to estimate means and covariances
REBALANCE_INTERVAL = 126                # semi-annual (126 trading days = 6 months)

COST = 0.0010               # 10 bps (0.10%) per unit traded
RISK_AVERSION = 3           # Markowitz lambda

2. Data: prices, simple returns and risk-free rate¶

  • We use simple returns $R_t = P_t / P_{t-1} - 1$ because the return of a portfolio is the weighted average of the simple returns of the assets (with log returns this is not true).
  • Adjusted prices already include dividends and splits. All the stocks are in USD and listed on US exchanges, so there is no currency conversion and the calendar is the same (we used the SPY calendar in notebook 01).
  • SPY vs ^GSPC: ^GSPC is the S&P 500 index — it is not investable and its price does not include dividends. SPY is an ETF that can be bought (it has management fees of ~0.09%/year) and its adjusted price includes dividends. That is why the market benchmark in the backtest is SPY.

Universe summary (full period)¶

Before comparing strategies, we look at the characteristics of each stock: annualised return and volatility, maximum drawdown and average correlation with the other stocks. Low correlations = more room to diversify.

def max_drawdown(r):
    # Largest fall from a previous peak of wealth (a negative number). Wealth starts at 1, and that 1 also counts
    # as a peak, so a fall on the very first day is counted too. The same function is used for every portfolio.
    wealth = (1 + r).cumprod()
    peak = wealth.cummax().clip(lower=1.0)
    return (wealth / peak - 1).min()


rows = []
for stock in stocks + ['SPY']:
    r = returns[stock].dropna()
    wealth = (1 + r).cumprod()
    rows.append({
        'Ticker': stock,
        'Sector': sector.get(stock, 'ETF (benchmark)'),
        'First date': r.index.min().date(),
        'Ann. return (CAGR)': wealth.iloc[-1] ** (252 / len(r)) - 1,
        'Ann. volatility': r.std() * np.sqrt(252),
        'Max drawdown': max_drawdown(r),
        'Avg. correlation with the other stocks': (correlations.loc[stock].sum() - 1) / (len(stocks) - 1) if stock in stocks else np.nan,
    })

Risk-free rate: 3-year Treasury yield (FRED DGS3)¶

The code tries to read the file data/risk_free_DGS3.csv. If it does not exist yet, it downloads the series from FRED and saves it (extraction date = the date on which this code is run; it is recorded in the file data/risk_free_DGS3_info.txt; if the download fails and you download the CSV by hand, write down the download date).

  • The series is in % per year (e.g. 4.25 = 4.25%) → we divide by 100.
  • On days when the stock market is open but the bond market is closed (e.g. Columbus Day), we use the last known value.
  • Daily rate = annual rate / 252.
In [6]:

3. The 8 strategies (and the Group pick)¶

Notation: $w$ = vector of weights, $\mu$ = annualised expected returns, $\Sigma$ = annualised covariance matrix, $\sigma_i$ = volatility of asset i, $C$ = correlation matrix, $r_f$ = risk-free rate. Common constraints: $w_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i w_i = 1$.

Strategy Objective Uses $\mu$? Uses $\Sigma$?
EW $w_i = 1/N$ no no
Markowitz (λ = 3) $\max_w \; w^\top\mu - \frac{\lambda}{2}\, w^\top\Sigma w$ yes yes
GMV $\min_w \; w^\top\Sigma w$ no yes
Max Sharpe $\max_w \; (w^\top\mu - r_f)\,/\,\sqrt{w^\top\Sigma w}$ yes yes
Inverse vol $w_i \propto 1/\sigma_i$ no only the diagonal
Risk parity (ERC) equal risk contributions: $w_i(\Sigma w)_i / w^\top\Sigma w = 1/N$ no yes
Most diversified $\max_w \; DR = w^\top\sigma \,/\, \sqrt{w^\top\Sigma w}$ no yes
Max decorrelation $\min_w \; w^\top C\, w$ no only the correlations

Why is Markowitz different from GMV and Max Sharpe? With λ = 3 the investor accepts some risk in exchange for return: as λ → ∞ Markowitz gets closer to GMV; with a small λ it moves towards the asset with the highest expected return. Max Sharpe is the point of the frontier that is tangent to the risk-free rate, which in general does not coincide with λ = 3 (see the chart in section 4).

Inverse vol vs ERC: both give more weight to the less volatile assets, but inverse vol ignores correlations. They are only the same if all the correlations are equal. With different correlations, ERC gives less weight to the assets that are highly correlated with the others.

The optimisers use scipy.optimize.minimize with the SLSQP method (it accepts bounds and equality constraints). If SLSQP reports a failure, the optimisation is repeated once with a looser tolerance (ftol = 1e-8); if it fails again, equal weights are used at that rebalancing and the failure is recorded (04_optimisation_failures.csv, section 13).

In [7]:
def estimate_parameters(sample):
    # ANNUALISED mean (vector) and covariance (matrix) from daily returns
    mu = sample.mean().values * DAYS_PER_YEAR
    sigma = sample.cov().values * DAYS_PER_YEAR
    return mu, sigma


failure_log = []   # here we store the optimisations that fail (the brief asks us not to hide them)
retry_log = []     # optimisations that failed at the first attempt but worked at the second one


def optimise(objective_function, n_assets, name, initial_weights=None, min_weight=0.0):
    # Minimises 'objective_function' subject to: min_weight <= w_i <= 1 and sum of weights = 1
    if initial_weights is None:
        initial_weights = np.ones(n_assets) / n_assets          # start from equally weighted

    bounds = [(min_weight, 1)] * n_assets
    sum_constraint = {'type': 'eq', 'fun': lambda w: np.sum(w) - 1}

    # ftol = precision requested from the optimiser. With values that are too small (e.g. 1e-12) SLSQP sometimes
    # is already at the optimum but reports a failure; 1e-10 is precise and almost always converges.
    result = minimize(objective_function, initial_weights, method='SLSQP',
                      bounds=bounds, constraints=[sum_constraint],
                      options={'maxiter': 1000, 'ftol': 1e-10})

    if not result.success:
        retry_log.append({'Strategy': name, 'Message': result.message})   # first attempt failed
        # Second attempt with a slightly looser precision (1e-8). Sometimes SLSQP stops right next to the optimum
        # and reports a failure; whether that happens can depend on the computer / library version, so this retry
        # makes the results more stable across computers.
        result = minimize(objective_function, initial_weights, method='SLSQP',
                          bounds=bounds, constraints=[sum_constraint],
                          options={'maxiter': 1000, 'ftol': 1e-8})

    if not result.success:
        # Plan B: if it still fails, we use equally weighted and record the failure
        failure_log.append({'Strategy': name, 'Message': result.message})
        return np.ones(n_assets) / n_assets

    weights = np.clip(result.x, 0, None)   # remove tiny numerical negatives (e.g. -1e-15)
    return weights / weights.sum()

Each strategy is a function that receives the estimation sample (daily returns of the rolling window) and the annual risk-free rate and returns a vector of weights. Note: in Python, @ is the matrix product (e.g. w @ sigma @ w = $w^\top\Sigma w$ = portfolio variance).

In [8]:
# a) Equally weighted
def weights_equal_weight(sample, rf):
    n = sample.shape[1]
    return np.ones(n) / n


# b) Markowitz mean-variance with risk aversion lambda
def weights_markowitz(sample, rf, aversion=RISK_AVERSION):
    mu, sigma = estimate_parameters(sample)

    def objective(w):
        utility = w @ mu - aversion / 2 * (w @ sigma @ w)
        return -utility                     # minimising the negative = maximising the utility

    return optimise(objective, len(mu), 'Markowitz')


# c) Global minimum variance
def weights_min_variance(sample, rf):
    mu, sigma = estimate_parameters(sample)

    def objective(w):
        return w @ sigma @ w                # portfolio variance

    return optimise(objective, len(mu), 'GMV')


# d) Max Sharpe (tangency portfolio)
def weights_max_sharpe(sample, rf):
    mu, sigma = estimate_parameters(sample)

    # Safety rule: if NO stock is expected to beat the risk-free rate, the "tangency" portfolio does not exist
    # (maximising a negative ratio would just pick the most volatile stocks). Then we use GMV and log it.
    # (It never happens in our runs: the failure log stays empty.)
    if np.all(mu <= rf):
        failure_log.append({'Strategy': 'Max Sharpe', 'Message': 'no stock with expected return above rf -> GMV weights used'})
        return weights_min_variance(sample, rf)

    def objective(w):
        sharpe = (w @ mu - rf) / np.sqrt(w @ sigma @ w)
        return -sharpe

    return optimise(objective, len(mu), 'Max Sharpe')
In [9]:
# e1) Inverse volatility (no optimiser needed)
def weights_inverse_vol(sample, rf):
    vol = sample.std().values
    return (1 / vol) / np.sum(1 / vol)


def risk_contributions(w, sigma):
    # Share of the total portfolio risk that comes from each asset (sum = 1)
    variance = w @ sigma @ w
    return w * (sigma @ w) / variance


# e2) Risk parity / Equal Risk Contribution
def weights_risk_parity(sample, rf):
    mu, sigma = estimate_parameters(sample)
    n = len(mu)

    def objective(w):
        # sum of the squared differences between each asset's contribution and 1/N
        return np.sum((risk_contributions(w, sigma) - 1 / n) ** 2)

    # We start from the inverse vol weights (already close to the solution) and force every weight to be > 0,
    # because in ERC every asset must contribute to the risk.
    start_weights = weights_inverse_vol(sample, rf)
    return optimise(objective, n, 'Risk parity (ERC)', initial_weights=start_weights, min_weight=1e-6)
In [10]:
def diversification_ratio(w, sigma):
    # DR = weighted average of the volatilities / portfolio volatility  (>= 1; higher = more diversified)
    vol = np.sqrt(np.diag(sigma))
    return (w @ vol) / np.sqrt(w @ sigma @ w)


# f1) Most diversified portfolio
def weights_most_diversified(sample, rf):
    mu, sigma = estimate_parameters(sample)

    def objective(w):
        return -diversification_ratio(w, sigma)

    return optimise(objective, len(mu), 'Most diversified')


# f2) Maximum decorrelation: it is the "minimum variance" but using the CORRELATION matrix
#     (as if every asset had the same volatility)
def weights_max_decorrelation(sample, rf):
    correlation = sample.corr().values

    def objective(w):
        return w @ correlation @ w

    return optimise(objective, correlation.shape[0], 'Max decorrelation')

The Group pick (23 stocks): the group's own portfolio¶

Besides the 8 strategies of the brief, we test the portfolio that the group itself chose: the 23 S&P 500 stocks selected in notebook 01 (by GICS sector), each with the same weight — 1/23 ≈ 4.35% (1/22 ≈ 4.55% in the experiments whose 3-year window starts on or before 2010-06-29, when TSLA has no data yet). It is rebalanced exactly like every other strategy: semi-annual, the same warm-up rebalancing, weights that drift between rebalancings, the same 10 bps cost on turnover, the same out-of-sample evaluation year and the same metrics.

Why is it a different portfolio from strategy a) EW? Both use equal weights (in the code they even use the same function, weights_equal_weight), but they hold different stocks:

a) EW Group pick (23 stocks)
Stocks held in each experiment the 12 stocks drawn at random for that experiment always the group's full 23-stock pick (all the stocks with data in the period)
Weight of each stock 1/12 ≈ 8.3% 1/23 ≈ 4.35% (1/22 before TSLA has data)
What it tests an allocation rule (1/N) applied to a given set of stocks holding all the group's stocks in equal weights

So EW and the 7 optimised strategies answer "how should we weight a given set of stocks?", while the Group pick answers "how does our full 23-stock universe do, held in equal weights?". Careful: EW's 12 stocks are drawn from the same 23, so the Group pick vs EW comparison measures the effect of holding 23 stocks instead of 12 (more diversification), not stock-picking skill. The Group pick is one more portfolio in every comparison, next to the 8 strategies and SPY (10 portfolios in total).

In [11]:
# Dictionary with all the strategies: name -> function

    'Max Sharpe': weights_max_sharpe,
    'Inverse vol': weights_inverse_vol,
    'Risk parity (ERC)': weights_risk_parity,
    'Most diversified': weights_most_diversified,
    'Max decorrelation': weights_max_decorrelation,
}

# The group's own portfolio: equal weights in ALL the 23 stocks (it uses the same function as EW, only the stocks change)

Note on the Group pick. In this illustration we use the full 23-stock universe, so the Group pick's weights (1/23 ≈ 4.35% in every stock) are exactly the EW weights (the EW column above). The two portfolios only differ in the backtest: there, EW is applied to the 12 randomly drawn stocks of each experiment, while the Group pick always holds all 23 (22 before TSLA has data). So any difference between EW and the Group pick in the backtest comes from the universe (fixed 23 vs random 12), not from the weighting rule.

Inverse vol vs Risk parity (ERC): risk contributions¶

In inverse vol the weights are proportional to $1/\sigma_i$, but the contributions to risk are not equal, because the assets that are more correlated with the rest of the portfolio contribute more. ERC corrects this.

Efficient frontier (in-sample)¶

We compute the long-only frontier: for each target return, the portfolio with the lowest variance. We mark the 8 strategies and Markowitz with λ = 1, 3 and 5 to show that it is different from GMV and Max Sharpe.

In [18]:
n = len(stocks)
gmv_return = illustration_weights['GMV'].values @ mu_illus
targets = np.linspace(gmv_return, mu_illus.max(), 40)

frontier_vol = []
for target in targets:
    constraints = [{'type': 'eq', 'fun': lambda w: np.sum(w) - 1},
                   {'type': 'eq', 'fun': lambda w: w @ mu_illus - target}]     # portfolio return = target
    res = minimize(lambda w: w @ sigma_illus @ w, np.ones(n) / n, method='SLSQP',
                   bounds=[(0, 1)] * n, constraints=constraints, options={'maxiter': 1000})
    frontier_vol.append(np.sqrt(res.fun))

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(frontier_vol, targets, color=COLOURS['reference'], linewidth=1.6, label='Efficient frontier (long-only)')
plt.scatter(np.sqrt(np.diag(sigma_illus)), mu_illus, color=COLOURS['axis'], edgecolor=COLOURS['muted'], s=36, label='Individual stocks')

for name in strategies.keys():
    w = illustration_weights[name].values
    # white edge around each point, so that points that are close to each other stay visible
    plt.scatter(np.sqrt(w @ sigma_illus @ w), w @ mu_illus, color=colours[name], s=90, edgecolor=COLOURS['background'], zorder=3, label=name)

for aversion in [1, 5]:

    name = f'Markowitz (λ={aversion})'
    plt.scatter(np.sqrt(w @ sigma_illus @ w), w @ mu_illus, color=colour(name), marker='^', s=70,
                edgecolor=COLOURS['background'], zorder=3, label=name)
    plt.annotate(f'λ={aversion}', (np.sqrt(w @ sigma_illus @ w), w @ mu_illus), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(6, -10),
                 color=COLOURS['text_secondary'])

Warning: this illustration is in-sample — it uses 1-year historical means as if they were the future. The strategies that depend on $\mu$ (Markowitz and Max Sharpe) concentrate on the stocks that rose the most in the last year. That is exactly why we need the out-of-sample backtest: to see whether this apparent advantage holds in the following year.

5. Design of the 100 experiments¶

For each experiment we draw:

  1. One contiguous 3-year period (756 trading days) within 2010–2026 — the chronological order is kept;
  2. 12 stocks among those with complete data in that period (eligibility: TSLA is only eligible in periods that start after 29/06/2010).

We use the same sample (period + stocks) for every strategy, and the seed is recorded → the result is reproducible.

The Group pick uses the same 100 periods (the same start_index), but it does not draw stocks: it always holds all the eligible stocks of the period (23, or 22 when the 3-year window starts on or before 2010-06-29, because TSLA has no data yet). Its design table, design_all, is built right after the main one without any random call, so the random draws of the 100 experiments are exactly the same as before.

In [19]:
# np.random.seed: with the same seed, NumPy guarantees the same sequence of numbers on any version/computer
np.random.seed(SEED)
dates = returns.index
n_days = len(dates)

rows = []
for e in range(1, N_EXPERIMENTS + 1):
    # 1) draw the first day of the 3-year period (the whole period must fit inside the data)
    start = int(np.random.randint(0, n_days - DATASET_DAYS + 1))
    end = start + DATASET_DAYS                        # exclusive

    # 2) eligible stocks = no missing values in the period
    block = returns[stocks].iloc[start:end]
    eligible = [stock for stock in stocks if block[stock].notna().all()]

    # 3) draw 12 stocks (without replacement)
    chosen = sorted(str(a) for a in np.random.choice(eligible, size=N_ASSETS, replace=False))

    rows.append({
        'Experiment': e,
        'start_index': start,
        'Estimation start': dates[start].date(),
        'Evaluation start': dates[start + EVAL_START].date(),
        'Evaluation end': dates[end - 1].date(),
        'N eligible': len(eligible),
        'Assets': chosen,
    })

Important note: the sampled periods overlap (there are only ~16 years of data, so there are at most ~14 different evaluation years). The 100 experiments are not 100 independent tests — they are used to look at the distribution of the results and at whether the conclusions depend on the period or on the stocks drawn, and not to run significance tests as if they were independent.

6. Simulating one strategy in one experiment¶

For each experiment and strategy:

  1. Rebalancing dates: every 126 days. The first one is one semester before the start of the evaluation (warm-up): this way, on the 1st evaluation day the portfolio already exists and the turnover on that day is realistic (it is not a purchase made from cash). The warm-up returns are not included in the metrics.
  2. At each rebalancing, the weights are computed using only the previous 252 days (no look-ahead). Trades are made at the close of the previous day, i.e. the new weights apply from day t onwards (market-on-close convention: we trade at the closing price of the day on which we know the last observation).
  3. Turnover = $\sum_i |w_i^{target} - w_i^{before}|$ (purchases + sales, as a % of the portfolio).
  4. Between rebalancings the weights drift: $w_{i,t+1} = w_{i,t}(1+R_{i,t}) / (1+R_{p,t})$.
  5. Net return on the rebalancing day = gross return − cost × turnover.
In [22]:
def simulate(block_returns, rf_block, weight_function, interval=REBALANCE_INTERVAL, window=ESTIMATION_WINDOW, lag=0):
    # block_returns: DataFrame with 756 days x the stocks of the experiment (12, or 22-23 for the Group pick), simple returns
    # rf_block: Series with 756 days of ANNUAL risk-free rate
    # Returns a dictionary with the gross returns and the turnover of each day of the evaluation year,
    # and the target weights / diversification ratio of each rebalancing in the evaluation year.
    R = block_returns.values                 # numpy is faster inside a loop
    n_assets = R.shape[1]

    # Rebalancing days (the 1st is one interval before the start of the evaluation = warm-up)
    rebalance_days = list(range(EVAL_START - interval, DATASET_DAYS, interval))
    if rebalance_days[0] - window - lag < 0:
        raise ValueError('The estimation window does not fit before the 1st rebalancing')

    weights = np.zeros(n_assets)            # we start in cash
    gross_returns = []
    daily_turnover = []
    target_weights = []
    div_ratios = []

    for t in range(rebalance_days[0], DATASET_DAYS):
        turnover = 0.0

        if t in rebalance_days:
            # 1) estimate using only PAST data (days t-window to t-1)
            #    lag = 0 (main convention): we trade at the close of t-1, the last price used in the estimation
            #    lag = 1 (robustness, section 10.7): the estimation stops one day earlier (days t-window-1 to t-2)
            sample = block_returns.iloc[t - window - lag:t - lag]
            known_rf = rf_block.iloc[t - 1 - lag]
            n_failures_before = len(failure_log)
            target = weight_function(sample, known_rf)
            for failure in failure_log[n_failures_before:]:          # if the optimisation failed, store the date
                failure['Rebalance date'] = block_returns.index[t].date()

            # 2) how much we need to trade to move from the current weights to the target
            turnover = np.sum(np.abs(target - weights))
            weights = target

            if t >= EVAL_START:
                target_weights.append(target)
                div_ratios.append(diversification_ratio(target, sample.cov().values))

        # 3) portfolio return on day t
        r_portfolio = np.sum(weights * R[t])

        # 4) the weights drift with prices until the next rebalancing
        weights = weights * (1 + R[t]) / (1 + r_portfolio)

        # 5) we only store the evaluation year
        if t >= EVAL_START:
            gross_returns.append(r_portfolio)
            daily_turnover.append(turnover)

    eval_dates = block_returns.index[EVAL_START:]
    return {
        'r_gross': pd.Series(gross_returns, index=eval_dates),
        'turnover': pd.Series(daily_turnover, index=eval_dates),
        'weights': target_weights,
        'div_ratio': div_ratios,
    }

7. Performance metrics (conventions)¶

Computed on the daily returns of the evaluation year (252 days):

Metric Formula / convention
Annualised return $\left(\prod_t (1+R_t)\right)^{252/n} - 1$ (geometric)
Annualised volatility $\text{standard deviation}(R_t)\times\sqrt{252}$
Sharpe $\overline{(R_t - r_{f,t})} \,/\, \text{sd}(R_t - r_{f,t}) \times \sqrt{252}$
Sortino $\overline{(R_t - r_{f,t})} \,/\, DD \times \sqrt{252}$, with $DD = \sqrt{\text{mean}(\min(R_t - r_{f,t}, 0)^2)}$
Maximum drawdown (MDD) largest fall from a previous peak of wealth (which starts at 1)
Calmar annualised return / |MDD|
Sterling annualised return / (|MDD| + 10%) — 1-year variant of the original ratio, which averages the annual MDDs of 3 years. With one evaluation year the 10% is about half of the denominator (the median |MDD| is ≈ 11%), so this Sterling ranks the portfolios almost like the return does; Calmar (return / |MDD|) is therefore also reported in every comparison
Annual turnover sum of the turnover of the rebalancings in the evaluation year
Cost drag gross annualised return − net annualised return
Effective N $1/\sum_i w_i^2$ (average across rebalancings): N = equal weights (12 for the 8 strategies, 22–23 for the Group pick), 1 = everything in one stock
Max weight largest target weight in the portfolio (average across rebalancings)
Diversification ratio (ex-ante) $w^\top\sigma / \sqrt{w^\top\Sigma w}$ computed with the estimation sample (the 252 days before the rebalancing), averaged across rebalancings. It is an ex-ante (in-sample) measure, not an out-of-sample result — Most diversified has the highest value by construction

The ratios use the risk-free rate of each day (Sharpe, Sortino). Calmar and Sterling use the annualised return (without subtracting the risk-free rate), as in the original definitions.

In [23]:
def compute_metrics(r, rf_d):
    # r: daily portfolio returns | rf_d: daily risk-free rate on the same dates
    excess = r - rf_d
    n = len(r)

    wealth = (1 + r).cumprod()
    ann_return = wealth.iloc[-1] ** (DAYS_PER_YEAR / n) - 1
    ann_vol = r.std() * np.sqrt(DAYS_PER_YEAR)

    sharpe = excess.mean() / excess.std() * np.sqrt(DAYS_PER_YEAR)

    downside_dev = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.minimum(excess, 0) ** 2))
    sortino = excess.mean() / downside_dev * np.sqrt(DAYS_PER_YEAR)

    mdd = max_drawdown(r)                                   # negative number (function defined in section 2)

    calmar = ann_return / abs(mdd) if mdd < 0 else np.nan
    sterling = ann_return / (abs(mdd) + 0.10)

    return {
        'Ann. return': ann_return,
        'Ann. volatility': ann_vol,
        'Sharpe': sharpe,
        'Sortino': sortino,
        'Max drawdown': mdd,
        'Calmar': calmar,
        'Sterling': sterling,
    }
In [24]:
def metrics_table(simulations, cost, design_table=None):
    # Turns the simulations into a table: one row per (experiment, strategy)
    # design_table: by default uses the main design of the experiments
    if design_table is None:
        design_table = design

    rows = []
    for (e, name), sim in simulations.items():
        rf_d = rf_daily.loc[sim['r_gross'].index]

        r_net = sim['r_gross'] - cost * sim['turnover']
        m_net = compute_metrics(r_net, rf_d)
        m_gross = compute_metrics(sim['r_gross'], rf_d)

        row = {'Experiment': e, 'Strategy': name}
        row.update(m_net)                                  # metrics net of costs
        row['Ann. return (gross)'] = m_gross['Ann. return']
        row['Sharpe (gross)'] = m_gross['Sharpe']
        row['Cost drag'] = m_gross['Ann. return'] - m_net['Ann. return']
        row['Turnover (annual)'] = sim['turnover'].sum()
        row['Effective N'] = np.mean([1 / np.sum(w ** 2) for w in sim['weights']])
        row['Max weight'] = np.mean([w.max() for w in sim['weights']])
        row['Diversification ratio (ex-ante)'] = np.mean(sim['div_ratio'])
        rows.append(row)

    # Market benchmark: SPY bought at the start of the evaluation year and held (no rebalancing costs)
    for e in design_table.index:
        start = design_table.loc[e, 'start_index']
        eval_dates = returns.index[start + EVAL_START: start + DATASET_DAYS]
        m_spy = compute_metrics(returns.loc[eval_dates, 'SPY'], rf_daily.loc[eval_dates])
        row = {'Experiment': e, 'Strategy': 'SPY (buy & hold)'}
        row.update(m_spy)
        row['Ann. return (gross)'] = m_spy['Ann. return']
        row['Sharpe (gross)'] = m_spy['Sharpe']
        row['Cost drag'] = 0.0
        row['Turnover (annual)'] = 0.0
        rows.append(row)

    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def run_backtest(strategy_dict, interval=REBALANCE_INTERVAL, design_table=None, run_name='Main', lag=0):
    # Runs every strategy in every experiment. Returns a dictionary (experiment, strategy) -> simulation
    # run_name: identifies this run in the optimisation failure log
    if design_table is None:
        design_table = design

    simulations = {}
    for e in design_table.index:
        start = design_table.loc[e, 'start_index']
        assets_e = design_table.loc[e, 'Assets']
        block = returns[assets_e].iloc[start:start + DATASET_DAYS]
        rf_block = rf_annual.iloc[start:start + DATASET_DAYS]

        for name, function in strategy_dict.items():
            n_failures_before = len(failure_log)
            simulations[(e, name)] = simulate(block, rf_block, function, interval=interval, lag=lag)
            for failure in failure_log[n_failures_before:]:       # identify the failures of this simulation
                failure['Run'] = run_name
                failure['Experiment'] = e
                failure['Strategy'] = name                        # full name, e.g. 'Markowitz (λ=1)'
    return simulations


def show_failures(run_name):
    # Shows the optimisations that failed in one run (on those rebalancings we used equal weights)
    failures = [f for f in failure_log if f.get('Run') == run_name]
    print(f'Optimisations that failed ({run_name}): {len(failures)}')
    if len(failures) > 0:
        display(pd.DataFrame(failures))

8. Running the main backtest (semi-annual rebalancing, 10 bps)¶

  1. The 8 strategies run on the 100 experiments of design (12 random stocks each).
  2. The Group pick runs on the same 100 experiments with design_all: the same periods, the same rebalancing dates, warm-up, costs and evaluation year, but all the eligible stocks (23, or 22 before TSLA) in equal weights. It is a different portfolio from EW, which holds only the 12 drawn stocks (see section 3).
  3. The Group pick simulations are merged into simulations, so every table and chart below has 10 portfolios (8 strategies + Group pick + SPY).

Check of the optimiser solutions. "0 failures" only means that SLSQP stopped normally, so we also check the weights themselves: in every rebalancing of the evaluation year they must add up to 1 and be ≥ 0, and ERC must give every stock the same share of the risk (1/N), using the same covariance matrix as the optimiser.

In [27]:
max_sum_error = 0.0     # largest |sum of weights - 1|
lowest_weight = 1.0     # smallest weight found
max_rc_gap = 0.0        # ERC: largest |risk contribution - 1/N|

for (e, name), sim in simulations.items():
    for w in sim['weights']:
        max_sum_error = max(max_sum_error, abs(w.sum() - 1))
        lowest_weight = min(lowest_weight, w.min())

    if name == 'Risk parity (ERC)':
        start = design.loc[e, 'start_index']
        block = returns[design.loc[e, 'Assets']].iloc[start:start + DATASET_DAYS]
        for k, w in enumerate(sim['weights']):
            t = EVAL_START + k * REBALANCE_INTERVAL                 # rebalancing day of this weight vector
            mu, sigma = estimate_parameters(block.iloc[t - ESTIMATION_WINDOW:t])
            rc = risk_contributions(w, sigma)
            max_rc_gap = max(max_rc_gap, np.max(np.abs(rc - 1 / len(w))))

print(f'Largest |sum of weights - 1|: {max_sum_error:.1e}')
print(f'Smallest weight: {lowest_weight:.1e}  (must be >= 0)')
print(f'ERC: largest |risk contribution - 1/N| = {max_rc_gap:.1e}  (1/N = {1/12:.4f} with 12 stocks)')

9.2 Dispersion across experiments and % of experiments in which each portfolio beats EW, the Group pick and SPY¶

The function beats_benchmark(table, benchmark) counts, for each portfolio, the % of experiments in which it is better than the benchmark in the same experiment (higher Sharpe, return, Sterling and Calmar; smaller drawdown; lower volatility). We use it with three benchmarks: EW (the main benchmark of the brief), the Group pick and SPY.

# The 5 metrics used to compare two portfolios: (column, True if a HIGHER value is better)
# (the maximum drawdown is negative, so a higher value = a smaller fall)
comparison_metrics = [('Sharpe', True), ('Ann. return', True), ('Max drawdown', True),
                      ('Ann. volatility', False), ('Sterling', True), ('Calmar', True)]


def beats_benchmark(table, benchmark, label=None, names=None):
    # % of experiments in which each portfolio is better than 'benchmark' in the SAME experiment
    # label: short name of the benchmark used in the column titles (e.g. 'Group pick')
    # names: the portfolios to show (rows); by default the 10 portfolios of 'order'
    if label is None:
        label = benchmark
    if names is None:
        names = order
    result = pd.DataFrame(index=names)
    for metric, higher_is_better in comparison_metrics:
        wide = table.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values=metric)   # experiments x portfolios
        for name in names:
            if name == benchmark:
                continue
            if higher_is_better:
                beats = wide[name] > wide[benchmark]       # True in the experiments in which 'name' is better
            else:
                beats = wide[name] < wide[benchmark]       # lower volatility is better
            result.loc[name, f'% beats {label}: {metric}'] = 100 * beats.mean()
    return result.drop(index=benchmark)

def draw_boxplot(ax, data, names):
    # One box per portfolio, filled with the portfolio's colour (the same look in every boxplot of this notebook):
    # grey outline, whiskers and caps, dark median line, small grey dots for the outliers
    box = ax.boxplot(data, patch_artist=True, showfliers=True,
                     boxprops=dict(edgecolor=COLOURS['text_secondary']),
                     whiskerprops=dict(color=COLOURS['text_secondary']),
                     capprops=dict(color=COLOURS['text_secondary']),
                     medianprops=dict(color=COLOURS['text'], linewidth=1.6),
                     flierprops=dict(marker='o', markersize=3, markerfacecolor=COLOURS['muted'], markeredgecolor=COLOURS['muted']))
    for patch, name in zip(box['boxes'], names):
        patch.set_facecolor(colours[name])
        patch.set_alpha(0.85)
    ax.set_xticks(range(1, len(names) + 1))
    ax.set_xticklabels(names, rotation=35, ha='right')
    ax.xaxis.grid(False)                 # no vertical gridlines (the x axis has categories)

9.5 Head-to-head comparison of all portfolios¶

Sections 9.2 and 9.4 compare each portfolio with one benchmark (EW, the Group pick or SPY) or rank them all at once. Here we compare every portfolio against every other one. All 10 portfolios are evaluated on the same 100 experiments (the same out-of-sample years), so for each pair of portfolios (A, B) we can count in how many experiments A was better than B:

$$W[A, B] = \% \text{ of the 100 experiments in which portfolio } A \text{ (row) is better than portfolio } B \text{ (column) in the same experiment}$$

  • Better = higher Sharpe ratio (net), higher annualised return (net), smaller maximum drawdown (less negative), lower annualised volatility, higher Sterling ratio (net).
  • $W[A, B] + W[B, A] = 100\%$ (ties are practically impossible). Above 50% → A beats B more often than not. The diagonal is left blank.
  • The last matrix is the median paired difference of the Sharpe ratio: the median, over the 100 experiments, of (Sharpe of A − Sharpe of B) in the same experiment — by how much A usually beats (or loses to) B.
  • Reading example: row Group pick (23 stocks), column EW of the Sharpe matrix = % of the experiments in which the Group pick had a higher Sharpe ratio than EW.
  • The last table summarises each row: the average % of head-to-head comparisons won against the other 9 portfolios.
  • Charts: the six matrices in one figure (04_pairwise_win_rates.png) and, larger and easier to read in the report, the Sharpe matrix on its own (04_pairwise_sharpe.png).
  • Reminder: the experiments overlap (section 5), so these percentages measure consistency, not statistical significance.
In [35]:
def pairwise_win_rates(table, metric, higher_is_better, names):
    # W[A, B] = % of experiments in which A (row) is better than B (column) in the SAME experiment
    wide = table.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values=metric)     # experiments x portfolios
    matrix = pd.DataFrame(np.nan, index=names, columns=names)
    for a in names:
        for b in names:
            if a == b:
                continue                                  # the diagonal stays empty (NaN)
            if higher_is_better:
                matrix.loc[a, b] = 100 * (wide[a] > wide[b]).mean()
            else:
                matrix.loc[a, b] = 100 * (wide[a] < wide[b]).mean()
    return matrix


def median_paired_difference(table, metric, names):
    # D[A, B] = median over the experiments of (metric of A - metric of B) in the SAME experiment
    wide = table.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values=metric)
    matrix = pd.DataFrame(np.nan, index=names, columns=names)
    for a in names:
        for b in names:
            if a != b:
                matrix.loc[a, b] = (wide[a] - wide[b]).median()
    return matrix

def plot_heatmap(ax, matrix, title, centre, limit, number_format):
    # Annotated heatmap: rows = portfolio A, columns = portfolio B; the empty diagonal (NaN) is left blank
    # Colours (two-colour scale with a grey middle at 'centre'): blue = the row portfolio A wins, orange-red = it loses
    image = ax.imshow(matrix.values.astype(float), cmap=diverging_cmap(), vmin=centre - limit, vmax=centre + limit)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(matrix.columns)))
    ax.set_xticklabels(matrix.columns, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=8)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(matrix.index)))
    ax.set_yticklabels(matrix.index, fontsize=8)
    for i in range(len(matrix.index)):
        for j in range(len(matrix.columns)):
            value = matrix.values[i, j]
            if not np.isnan(value):
                ax.text(j, i, format(value, number_format), ha='center', va='center', fontsize=8,
                        color=cell_text_colour(image, value))
    ax.grid(False)                                   # no gridlines on top of the coloured cells
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel('Portfolio B (column)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Portfolio A (row)')
    return image

9.7 Market risk: CAPM beta, Jensen's alpha, tracking error and information ratio (Lab 4.1)¶

So far we compared the portfolios with each other. Here we measure how much market risk each one takes and whether it earns more than the CAPM predicts for that risk. For each portfolio and each experiment we run, on the 252 daily returns of the evaluation year (net of costs), the CAPM regression of Lab 4.1 with SPY as the market:

$$R_{p,t} - r_{f,t} = \alpha + \beta\,(R_{SPY,t} - r_{f,t}) + \varepsilon_t$$

Measure Meaning
Beta ($\beta$) sensitivity to the market: β < 1 → the portfolio moves less than SPY (defensive)
Jensen's alpha ($\alpha \times 252$) annualised return not explained by the market risk taken (> 0 → better than the CAPM predicts)
Alpha t-stat $\alpha$ / standard error (OLS); |t| > 1.96 → significant at 5% in that experiment
R² share of the portfolio's daily variance explained by the market
Tracking error $\text{sd}(R_{p,t} - R_{SPY,t}) \times \sqrt{252}$: how far the portfolio deviates from SPY
Information ratio $\overline{(R_{p,t} - R_{SPY,t})} \times 252$ / tracking error: active return per unit of active risk

Notes: SPY itself has β = 1 and α = 0 by construction, so it is not shown. The OLS t-statistics assume independent errors with constant variance, which daily returns do not satisfy (volatility clustering, notebook 03), so read them only as a rough guide. As before, the 100 experiments overlap, so we look at medians and percentages, not at a joint significance test.

In [39]:
import statsmodels.api as sm

capm_rows = []
for (e, name), sim in simulations.items():
    dates = sim['r_gross'].index
    r_portfolio = sim['r_gross'] - COST * sim['turnover']        # net of costs, as in the other tables
    r_market = returns.loc[dates, 'SPY']
    rf_d = rf_daily.loc[dates]

    # CAPM regression on excess returns (as in Lab 4.1)
    y = r_portfolio - rf_d
    x = sm.add_constant(r_market - rf_d)                          # adds the column of ones for the alpha
    fit = sm.OLS(y, x).fit()

    # Active return = portfolio - SPY
    active = r_portfolio - r_market
    tracking_error = active.std() * np.sqrt(DAYS_PER_YEAR)

    capm_rows.append({
        'Experiment': e,
        'Strategy': name,
        'Beta': fit.params.iloc[1],
        'Alpha (ann.)': fit.params.iloc[0] * DAYS_PER_YEAR,       # daily alpha x 252
        'Alpha t-stat': fit.tvalues.iloc[0],
        'R²': fit.rsquared,
        'Tracking error': tracking_error,
        'Information ratio': active.mean() * DAYS_PER_YEAR / tracking_error,
    })

capm_results = pd.DataFrame(capm_rows)
capm_order = [name for name in order if name != 'SPY (buy & hold)']     # the 8 strategies and the Group pick

# Medians across the 100 experiments + a few percentages
capm_measures = ['Beta', 'Alpha (ann.)', 'Alpha t-stat', 'R²', 'Tracking error', 'Information ratio']
capm_medians = capm_results.groupby('Strategy')[capm_measures].median().loc[capm_order]
for name in capm_order:
    rows_of_portfolio = capm_results[capm_results['Strategy'] == name]
    capm_medians.loc[name, '% beta < 1'] = 100 * (rows_of_portfolio['Beta'] < 1).mean()
    capm_medians.loc[name, '% alpha > 0'] = 100 * (rows_of_portfolio['Alpha (ann.)'] > 0).mean()
    capm_medians.loc[name, '% alpha significant > 0 (t > 1.96)'] = 100 * (rows_of_portfolio['Alpha t-stat'] > 1.96).mean()
    # IR > 0 = higher average daily return than SPY in that year
    capm_medians.loc[name, '% IR > 0 (beats SPY)'] = 100 * (rows_of_portfolio['Information ratio'] > 0).mean()

print('CAPM against SPY - medians of the 100 experiments (net of 10 bps) and % of experiments')
display(capm_medians.round(2))

9.8 How sure are we? Overlapping experiments and uncertainty bands¶

The 100 out-of-sample years overlap: two experiments that start a few weeks apart share most of their days. So the 100 experiments are not 100 independent observations (the brief asks us not to treat them as such). Here we measure how much they overlap and put an uncertainty band around the most important "% of experiments" numbers.

How the band is computed (cluster bootstrap): we group the experiments by the calendar year in which their out-of-sample year starts (14 years, 2012-2025). We then draw 14 years at random with replacement (some years appear twice, others not at all), recompute the % of experiments won with the experiments of those years, and repeat 2,000 times. The band is the range that contains the middle 95% of the 2,000 results. Resampling whole years (and not single experiments) keeps the overlapping experiments together. A difference is called clear only when its band does not include 50%.

In [41]:
# (a) How much do the 100 out-of-sample years overlap?
coverage = pd.Series(0, index=returns.index)            # number of experiments that use each trading day out of sample
for e in design.index:
    start = design.loc[e, 'start_index']
    coverage.iloc[start + EVAL_START:start + DATASET_DAYS] += 1
covered_days = coverage[coverage > 0]
print(f'Each out-of-sample day belongs to {covered_days.mean():.1f} experiments on average '
      f'(between {covered_days.min()} and {covered_days.max()})')

# Largest group of experiments whose out-of-sample years do not overlap at all: go through the experiments by start date and
# keep one only if it starts after the end of the last one kept
last_end = -1
non_overlapping = []
for e in design.sort_values('start_index').index:
    eval_start = design.loc[e, 'start_index'] + EVAL_START
    if eval_start > last_end:
        non_overlapping.append(e)
        last_end = design.loc[e, 'start_index'] + DATASET_DAYS - 1
print('Largest number of experiments whose out-of-sample years do not overlap:', len(non_overlapping))

Each out-of-sample day belongs to 6.9 experiments on average (between 1 and 14)
Largest number of experiments whose out-of-sample years do not overlap: 13
In [42]:
# (b) Uncertainty bands for the most important comparisons (cluster bootstrap by year of the start of the out-of-sample year)
start_year = pd.to_datetime(design['Evaluation start']).dt.year
years = sorted(start_year.unique())
print('Out-of-sample years start in', len(years), 'different calendar years:', years[0], 'to', years[-1])

np.random.seed(SEED + 3)              # own seed for the bootstrap (it changes no other result of the notebook)
N_BOOTSTRAP = 2000


def win_rate_band(wins):
    # wins: True / False for each of the 100 experiments. Returns the % of wins and its 95% band.
    wins_per_year = wins.groupby(start_year).sum()               # number of wins in each start year
    experiments_per_year = wins.groupby(start_year).count()      # number of experiments in each start year
    rates = []
    for draw in range(N_BOOTSTRAP):
        chosen_years = np.random.choice(years, size=len(years), replace=True)
        rates.append(100 * wins_per_year[chosen_years].sum() / experiments_per_year[chosen_years].sum())
    return 100 * wins.mean(), np.percentile(rates, 2.5), np.percentile(rates, 97.5)


sharpe_w = results.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Sharpe')
vol_w = results.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Ann. volatility')
mdd_w = results.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Max drawdown')
ERC, IV, SPY_NAME = 'Risk parity (ERC)', 'Inverse vol', 'SPY (buy & hold)'

comparisons = [
    ('Group pick beats EW (Sharpe)', sharpe_w[GROUP] > sharpe_w['EW']),
    ('ERC beats EW (Sharpe)', sharpe_w[ERC] > sharpe_w['EW']),
    ('Inverse vol beats EW (Sharpe)', sharpe_w[IV] > sharpe_w['EW']),
    ('Most diversified beats EW (Sharpe)', sharpe_w['Most diversified'] > sharpe_w['EW']),
    ('Max decorrelation beats EW (Sharpe)', sharpe_w['Max decorrelation'] > sharpe_w['EW']),
    ('GMV beats EW (Sharpe)', sharpe_w['GMV'] > sharpe_w['EW']),
    ('Max Sharpe beats EW (Sharpe)', sharpe_w['Max Sharpe'] > sharpe_w['EW']),
    ('Markowitz beats EW (Sharpe)', sharpe_w['Markowitz (λ=3)'] > sharpe_w['EW']),
    ('ERC beats inverse vol (Sharpe)', sharpe_w[ERC] > sharpe_w[IV]),
    ('Group pick beats ERC (Sharpe)', sharpe_w[GROUP] > sharpe_w[ERC]),
    ('ERC lower volatility than EW', vol_w[ERC] < vol_w['EW']),
    ('ERC smaller drawdown than EW', mdd_w[ERC] > mdd_w['EW']),
    ('ERC beats SPY (Sharpe)', sharpe_w[ERC] > sharpe_w[SPY_NAME]),
    ('ERC lower volatility than SPY', vol_w[ERC] < vol_w[SPY_NAME]),
    ('ERC smaller drawdown than SPY', mdd_w[ERC] > mdd_w[SPY_NAME]),
    ('Group pick beats SPY (Sharpe)', sharpe_w[GROUP] > sharpe_w[SPY_NAME]),
    ('EW beats SPY (Sharpe)', sharpe_w['EW'] > sharpe_w[SPY_NAME]),
]

rows = []
for description, wins in comparisons:
    share, low, high = win_rate_band(wins)
    if low > 50 or high < 50:
        clear = 'yes'
    else:
        clear = 'no (band includes 50%)'
    rows.append({'Comparison': description, '% of experiments': share, 'Band low (95%)': low, 'Band high (95%)': high, 'Clear?': clear})
win_rate_bands = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('Comparison')
display(win_rate_bands.round(0))

10. Robustness¶

10.1 Higher transaction costs (0, 10, 25 and 50 bps)¶

There is no need to simulate again: we just recompute the net returns with a different cost (for the 8 strategies and the Group pick).

In [43]:
cost_levels = [0.0, 0.0010, 0.0025, 0.0050]

sharpe_by_cost = pd.DataFrame(index=order)
ranking_by_cost = pd.DataFrame(index=order)
avg_rank_by_cost = pd.DataFrame(index=order)
for cost in cost_levels:
    table_c = metrics_table(simulations, cost)
    label = f'{cost * 10000:.0f} bps'
    sharpe_by_cost[label] = table_c.groupby('Strategy')['Sharpe'].median()
    ranking_by_cost[label] = sharpe_by_cost[label].rank(ascending=False)
    # average of the rank in each experiment (more stable than the rank of the medians, see section 9.4)
    sharpe_c = table_c.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Sharpe')[order]
    avg_rank_by_cost[label] = sharpe_c.rank(axis=1, ascending=False).mean()

print('Median Sharpe ratio (net) for each cost level')
display(sharpe_by_cost.round(3))
print('Position in the ranking (by median Sharpe ratio)')
display(ranking_by_cost.astype(int))
print('Average rank in each experiment (1 = best of 10)')
display(avg_rank_by_cost.round(2))

             color=colours[name], label=name)

10.2 Quarterly rebalancing (convention suggested in the brief)¶

Same experiments, same strategies (and the Group pick, again on all the eligible stocks), but rebalancing every 63 days.

10.4 Do the results depend on the period?¶

(a) Sharpe ratio difference relative to EW in each experiment, over time (start date of the evaluation), for the 7 optimised strategies and the Group pick. (b) Medians by sub-period and by market regime (evaluation year with SPY going up or down). Each experiment is assigned to the sub-period that contains the middle of its evaluation year. Because medians of overlapping experiments move a lot when a few experiments change group, we also show the paired comparison (% of experiments that beat EW in the same experiment) by sub-period, and the drawdowns in the years in which SPY fell (the relevant evidence for a defensive strategy).

In [46]:

def sub_period(date):
    # Puts a date (the MIDDLE of the evaluation year) into one of 3 sub-periods
    if date.year < 2017:
        return '2012-2016'
    elif date.year < 2021:
        return '2017-2020'
    else:
        return '2021-2026'


# Market regime: did SPY go up or down in the evaluation year?
spy_return = results[results['Strategy'] == 'SPY (buy & hold)'].set_index('Experiment')['Ann. return']
regime = pd.Series(np.where(spy_return > 0, 'SPY up', 'SPY down'), index=spy_return.index)
# Each experiment is classified by the MIDDLE of its evaluation year (126 trading days after the start):
# an evaluation year that starts in November 2016 has most of its days in 2017, so it counts as 2017-2020
middle_dates = pd.Series([returns.index[design.loc[e, 'start_index'] + EVAL_START + 126] for e in design.index],
                         index=design.index)
period = middle_dates.apply(sub_period)

results['Sub-period'] = results['Experiment'].map(period)
results['Market regime'] = results['Experiment'].map(regime)

print('Number of experiments per sub-period:', period.value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())
print('Number of experiments per regime:', regime.value_counts().to_dict())

sharpe_period = pd.pivot_table(results, index='Strategy', columns='Sub-period', values='Sharpe', aggfunc='median').loc[order]
sharpe_regime = pd.pivot_table(results, index='Strategy', columns='Market regime', values='Sharpe', aggfunc='median').loc[order]
return_regime = pd.pivot_table(results, index='Strategy', columns='Market regime', values='Ann. return', aggfunc='median').loc[order]

print('\nMedian Sharpe ratio by sub-period')
display(sharpe_period.round(3))
print('Median Sharpe ratio by market regime')
display(sharpe_regime.round(3))
print('Median return by market regime')
display(return_regime.round(3))

# % of experiments in which each portfolio beats EW on the Sharpe ratio, in each sub-period
# (paired comparison in the same experiment, more informative than the medians above)
beats_ew_by_period = pd.DataFrame(index=[name for name in order if name != 'EW'])
for p in ['2012-2016', '2017-2020', '2021-2026']:
    subset = results[results['Sub-period'] == p]
    beats_ew_by_period[p] = beats_benchmark(subset, 'EW')['% beats EW: Sharpe']
print('% of experiments in which each portfolio has a higher Sharpe ratio than EW, by sub-period')
display(beats_ew_by_period.round(0))

# Years in which SPY fell: the relevant evidence for a defensive strategy is the DRAWDOWN, compared in the same experiment
down = results[results['Market regime'] == 'SPY down']
mdd_regime = pd.pivot_table(results, index='Strategy', columns='Market regime', values='Max drawdown', aggfunc='median').loc[order]
sharpe_down = down.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Sharpe')[order]
regime_drawdown = pd.DataFrame({
    'Median max drawdown (SPY down)': mdd_regime['SPY down'],
    'Median max drawdown (SPY up)': mdd_regime['SPY up'],
    '% smaller drawdown than EW (SPY down)': beats_benchmark(down, 'EW')['% beats EW: Max drawdown'],
    'Average Sharpe rank (SPY down)': sharpe_down.rank(axis=1, ascending=False).mean(),
}).loc[order]
print('Drawdowns in the years in which SPY fell (12 experiments) and in which it rose')
display(regime_drawdown.round(3))

10.5 Do the results depend on the stocks drawn?¶

Average weight given to each stock by each strategy (average across rebalancings, only in the experiments in which the stock was drawn). It shows where the money goes and whether the strategies depend on a few stocks.

The Group pick is excluded from this heatmap: its weights are trivially 1/23 ≈ 4.35% (1/22 before TSLA) in every stock, and its stocks are those of design_all (all the eligible stocks), not the 12 drawn stocks of design used here.

In [48]:
weight_sum = pd.DataFrame(0.0, index=stocks, columns=list(strategies.keys()))
weight_count = pd.DataFrame(0, index=stocks, columns=list(strategies.keys()))

for (e, name), sim in simulations.items():
    if name == GROUP:
        continue                                # excluded: equal weights in all the eligible stocks (see the text above)
    assets_e = design.loc[e, 'Assets']
    for w in sim['weights']:                    # one weight vector per rebalancing
        for stock, weight in zip(assets_e, w):
            weight_sum.loc[stock, name] += weight
            weight_count.loc[stock, name] += 1

avg_weight = weight_sum / weight_count

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 10))
image = ax.imshow(avg_weight.values * 100, cmap=sequential_cmap(), vmin=0, aspect='auto')   # white (0%) -> navy: darker = larger weight
ax.set_xticks(range(len(avg_weight.columns)))
ax.set_xticklabels(avg_weight.columns, rotation=35, ha='right')
ax.set_yticks(range(len(stocks)))
ax.set_yticklabels(stocks)
for i in range(len(stocks)):
    for j in range(len(avg_weight.columns)):
        value = avg_weight.values[i, j] * 100
        ax.text(j, i, f'{value:.0f}', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=8, color=cell_text_colour(image, value))
ax.grid(False)                                   # no gridlines on top of the coloured cells
plt.colorbar(image, label='Average weight when selected (%)')
ax.set_title('Average weight of each stock when selected (%) - equal weight would be 8.3%')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../figures/04_avg_weight_by_stock.png', dpi=150)
plt.show()

The same data as bars: one small panel per strategy, with the stocks in the same order in every panel and a line at the equal weight (1/12 ≈ 8.3%). Bars longer than the line = the strategy gives that stock more than an equal share. EW is left out because every one of its bars would be exactly on the line.

In [49]:
# The same data as the heatmap above (avg_weight), drawn as small multiples: one panel of horizontal bars per strategy
bar_strategies = [name for name in avg_weight.columns if name != 'EW']      # EW = 8.3% in every stock (it would only repeat the line)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(bar_strategies), figsize=(18, 7.5), sharey=True, sharex=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes, bar_strategies):

axes[0].invert_yaxis()                                   # the first stock at the top (sharey=True -> every panel follows)

10.6 Same periods, different stocks¶

To see whether the conclusions depend on the stocks drawn, we repeat the backtest with the same 100 periods but:

  • (a) a new draw of 12 stocks (a different seed). As there are only 23 stocks, the two draws have on average about half of their stocks in common;
  • (b) all the eligible stocks (22 or 23), i.e. without drawing stocks (the table design_all built in section 5).

If the ranking of the strategies changes a lot between the three versions, the conclusions depend on the subset of stocks.

The Group pick does not depend on the draw of 12 stocks (it always holds all the eligible stocks of the same periods), so in the three versions we reuse its simulations from section 8: its numbers are the same in every column, only its position relative to the other portfolios changes. In version (b), strategy a) EW is exactly the Group pick (equal weights in all the eligible stocks): the code checks that their numbers are identical, and in that column the two share the same rank (shown as x.5). There, the Group pick's "% beats EW" is 0%, because a portfolio never beats an identical copy of itself (it is a tie in every experiment, not a loss).

In [50]:
# (a) Same periods, DIFFERENT 12 stocks (a different seed, used only to draw the stocks)
np.random.seed(SEED + 1)
rows = []
for e in design.index:
    start = design.loc[e, 'start_index']
    block = returns[stocks].iloc[start:start + DATASET_DAYS]
    eligible = [stock for stock in stocks if block[stock].notna().all()]
    chosen = sorted(str(a) for a in np.random.choice(eligible, size=N_ASSETS, replace=False))
    rows.append({'Experiment': e, 'start_index': start, 'Assets': chosen})
design_new_draw = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('Experiment')

in_common = [len(set(a) & set(b)) for a, b in zip(design['Assets'], design_new_draw['Assets'])]
print('Average number of stocks in common with the main draw:', round(np.mean(in_common), 1), 'out of', N_ASSETS)

# (b) Same periods, ALL the eligible stocks: we reuse the table 'design_all' built in section 5

simulations_new_draw = run_backtest(strategies, design_table=design_new_draw, run_name='New draw of 12 stocks')
# The Group pick does not depend on the draw of 12 stocks: we reuse its simulations from section 8 (same periods)
for e in design.index:
    simulations_new_draw[(e, GROUP)] = simulations[(e, GROUP)]
results_new_draw = metrics_table(simulations_new_draw, COST, design_table=design_new_draw)
show_failures('New draw of 12 stocks')

simulations_all = run_backtest(strategies, design_table=design_all, run_name='All eligible stocks')
for e in design.index:
    simulations_all[(e, GROUP)] = simulations[(e, GROUP)]
results_all = metrics_table(simulations_all, COST, design_table=design_all)
show_failures('All eligible stocks')

# Check: with all the eligible stocks, EW IS the Group pick -> their numbers must be identical
check_columns = ['Ann. return', 'Ann. volatility', 'Sharpe', 'Sortino', 'Max drawdown', 'Calmar', 'Sterling',
                 'Turnover (annual)', 'Effective N', 'Max weight', 'Diversification ratio (ex-ante)']
ew_all = results_all[results_all['Strategy'] == 'EW'].set_index('Experiment')[check_columns]
group_all = results_all[results_all['Strategy'] == GROUP].set_index('Experiment')[check_columns]
largest_difference = (ew_all - group_all).abs().max().max()
print(f"\nLargest difference between EW and the Group pick in the 'All eligible stocks' run: {largest_difference}")
print('EW and the Group pick are identical in that run?', largest_difference == 0)

In [51]:
def short_summary(table):
    # Median Sharpe ratio, position in the ranking, median return and % of experiments that beat EW
    median_sharpe = table.groupby('Strategy')['Sharpe'].median()
    sharpe_by_experiment = table.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Sharpe')
    return pd.DataFrame({
        'Median Sharpe': median_sharpe,
        'Rank': median_sharpe.rank(ascending=False),
        'Average rank': sharpe_by_experiment.rank(axis=1, ascending=False).mean(),   # rank in each experiment, averaged
        'Median return': table.groupby('Strategy')['Ann. return'].median(),
        '% beats EW (Sharpe)': beats_benchmark(table, 'EW')['% beats EW: Sharpe'],
    })


subset_comparison = pd.concat({
    '12 stocks (main)': short_summary(results),
    '12 stocks (new draw)': short_summary(results_new_draw),
    'All eligible stocks': short_summary(results_all),
}, axis=1).loc[order]
display(subset_comparison.round(3))

# Agreement: in each experiment, does the strategy beat (or not) EW in BOTH samples of 12 stocks?
sharpe_main = results.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Sharpe')
sharpe_new_draw = results_new_draw.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Sharpe')
beats_main = sharpe_main.gt(sharpe_main['EW'], axis=0)
beats_new_draw = sharpe_new_draw.gt(sharpe_new_draw['EW'], axis=0)
agreement = 100 * (beats_main == beats_new_draw).mean()
print('% of experiments with the same conclusion "beats / does not beat EW" in the two samples of stocks:')
agreement_order = [name for name in order if name not in ['EW', 'SPY (buy & hold)']]     # same order as the other tables
subset_agreement = agreement.loc[agreement_order].to_frame('Agreement (%)')
display(subset_agreement.round(0))

10.7 Trading one day later (execution lag)¶

Main convention (section 6): the weights are computed with the data up to the close of day t-1 and traded at that same close. The brief asks to "execute trades after the information used to set the weights becomes available", and a real order must be sent before the closing price is known. Here we repeat the backtest with a one-day lag: the estimation window stops one day earlier (days t-253 to t-2, risk-free rate of t-2), and the new weights still apply from day t. Everything else is unchanged.

In [52]:
simulations_lag = run_backtest(strategies, run_name='One-day lag', lag=1)
simulations_lag.update(run_backtest({GROUP: weights_equal_weight}, design_table=design_all, run_name='One-day lag', lag=1))
results_lag = metrics_table(simulations_lag, COST)
show_failures('One-day lag')

sharpe_lag = results_lag.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Sharpe')
lag_comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    'Median Sharpe (main)': results.groupby('Strategy')['Sharpe'].median(),
    'Median Sharpe (1-day lag)': results_lag.groupby('Strategy')['Sharpe'].median(),
    'Median change in Sharpe (lag - main)': (sharpe_lag - sharpe_semi).median(),
    '% beats EW Sharpe (main)': beats_ew['% beats EW: Sharpe'],
    '% beats EW Sharpe (1-day lag)': beats_benchmark(results_lag, 'EW')['% beats EW: Sharpe'],
    'Average rank (main)': sharpe_semi[order].rank(axis=1, ascending=False).mean(),
    'Average rank (1-day lag)': sharpe_lag[order].rank(axis=1, ascending=False).mean(),
}).loc[order]
display(lag_comparison.round(3))

10.8 Without the five biggest winners (how much does choosing today's winners matter?)¶

The 23 stocks were chosen in 2026 among today's largest companies (section 14). The five stocks with the highest return over 2010-2026 are also among the most volatile ones. EW gives each of them 1/12 of the portfolio, while inverse vol, ERC and GMV give them less weight by design (they are volatile). So the hindsight in the choice of the universe does not affect all strategies equally: it flatters EW, Max decorrelation and Markowitz against the low-risk strategies.

To measure this, we repeat the backtest on the same 100 periods, drawing the 12 stocks only from the other 18 stocks. This is a sensitivity check (it uses hindsight in the opposite direction, removing the winners we know about), not an unbiased result.

In [53]:
# The five stocks with the highest full-sample return (CAGR 2010-2026, table of section 2)
top5 = universe_summary.drop(index='SPY').sort_values('Ann. return (CAGR)', ascending=False).index[:5].tolist()
others = [stock for stock in stocks if stock not in top5]
print('The five biggest winners of 2010-2026:', top5)

# Same periods (start_index of the main design), 12 stocks drawn from the other 18 (own seed)
np.random.seed(SEED + 2)
rows = []
for e in design.index:
    start = design.loc[e, 'start_index']
    block = returns[others].iloc[start:start + DATASET_DAYS]
    eligible = [stock for stock in others if block[stock].notna().all()]
    chosen = sorted(str(a) for a in np.random.choice(eligible, size=N_ASSETS, replace=False))
    rows.append({'Experiment': e, 'start_index': start, 'Assets': chosen})
design_without_top5 = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('Experiment')

simulations_without_top5 = run_backtest(strategies, design_table=design_without_top5, run_name='Without the 5 biggest winners')
results_without_top5 = metrics_table(simulations_without_top5, COST, design_table=design_without_top5)
show_failures('Without the 5 biggest winners')

names_without_top5 = list(strategies.keys()) + ['SPY (buy & hold)']     # no Group pick here (it holds all 23 stocks)
beats_spy_without = beats_benchmark(results_without_top5, 'SPY (buy & hold)', label='SPY', names=names_without_top5)
beats_ew_without = beats_benchmark(results_without_top5, 'EW', names=names_without_top5)
without_top5 = pd.DataFrame({
    'Median return (main)': results.groupby('Strategy')['Ann. return'].median(),
    'Median return (without top 5)': results_without_top5.groupby('Strategy')['Ann. return'].median(),
    'Median Sharpe (main)': results.groupby('Strategy')['Sharpe'].median(),
    'Median Sharpe (without top 5)': results_without_top5.groupby('Strategy')['Sharpe'].median(),
    '% lower volatility than SPY (main)': beats_spy['% beats SPY: Ann. volatility'],
    '% lower volatility than SPY (without top 5)': beats_spy_without['% beats SPY: Ann. volatility'],
    '% smaller drawdown than SPY (main)': beats_spy['% beats SPY: Max drawdown'],
    '% smaller drawdown than SPY (without top 5)': beats_spy_without['% beats SPY: Max drawdown'],
    '% beats SPY Sharpe (without top 5)': beats_spy_without['% beats SPY: Sharpe'],
    '% beats EW Sharpe (without top 5)': beats_ew_without['% beats EW: Sharpe'],
}).loc[names_without_top5]
display(without_top5.round(3))

return_without = results_without_top5.pivot(index='Experiment', columns='Strategy', values='Ann. return')

11. The guideline strategies applied to the group's 23-stock universe¶

Question: on our own 23 stocks, would an optimiser have beaten our equal-weight pick?

In the main backtest the 8 strategies work with 12 random stocks, while the Group pick holds all 23, so part of the difference between them comes from the universe. Here we put them on the same universe: we reuse the 'All eligible stocks' run of section 10.6 (the same 100 periods, all the eligible stocks — 23, or 22 before TSLA — semi-annual rebalancing, 10 bps, the same evaluation year). In that run strategy a) EW is the Group pick (identical numbers, checked in section 10.6), so it appears only once, as Group pick (23 stocks); the other rows are the 7 optimised strategies and SPY.

In [54]:

12. The Group pick over the full sample (2010-2026)¶

Warning — look-ahead and survivorship bias. The 23 stocks were chosen in 2026, by today's market capitalisation: they are the companies that survived and became the largest of their sectors (NVDA, AVGO, LLY, …). Nobody could have picked exactly these 23 stocks in January 2010. This full-sample history is therefore heavily affected by look-ahead and survivorship bias and it is NOT evidence that the pick would have beaten the market in real time. It is shown only as a description of what the pick did. The fair tests are the out-of-sample experiments (sections 9–11), where the Group pick competes with strategies built from the same stocks; even there, its advantage over SPY keeps part of this selection bias (section 14).

How the Group pick is simulated here (the same rules as in the backtest, but on the whole period instead of 1-year evaluation windows):

  • all the trading days from the start of the data (first return on 2010-01-05) to 2026-09-18;
  • equal weights among the stocks that have a price on the rebalancing date (the close at which we trade): 22 stocks at the start, TSLA joins at the first semi-annual rebalancing after its listing (29 June 2010);
  • semi-annual rebalancing every 126 trading days (the first one is the initial purchase), weights drift in between, 10 bps on the traded value (the initial purchase is also charged);
  • comparison with SPY (investable, total return because the adjusted price includes dividends) and ^GSPC (the S&P 500 price index: not investable and without dividends, so it understates the return of the market by about 1.5–2% per year).

Metrics: CAGR, annualised volatility, Sharpe (with the DGS3 rate of each day), Sortino, maximum drawdown, Calmar (CAGR / |MDD|) and Sterling. With 16+ years of data, Sterling uses its original definition: CAGR / (|average of the calendar-year maximum drawdowns| + 10%) (17 calendar years, 2010–2026; 2026 is year to date, until 18 September).

In [56]:
FULL_SAMPLE_END = pd.Timestamp('2026-09-18')

full_returns = returns.loc[:FULL_SAMPLE_END, stocks]
full_dates = full_returns.index
R_full = full_returns.fillna(0).values      # TSLA before its listing: return 0, but its weight is also 0, so nothing changes

# Alignment check: the return of day t goes from the close of prices.index[t] to the close of prices.index[t + 1]
# -> prices.iloc[t] is the close of the day BEFORE full_dates[t], i.e. the close at which we trade
assert prices.index[1] == full_dates[0]

full_rebalance_days = list(range(0, len(full_dates), REBALANCE_INTERVAL))      # every 126 days, starting on the 1st day

weights = np.zeros(len(stocks))              # we start in cash
gross_returns = []
daily_turnover = []
rebalance_log = []
for t in range(len(full_dates)):
    turnover = 0.0
    if t in full_rebalance_days:
        # 1) the stocks that can be bought: those with a price at the close at which we trade
        has_price = prices[stocks].iloc[t].notna().values
        target = has_price / has_price.sum()                    # 1/N among the stocks with a price
        # 2) traded value and new weights
        turnover = np.sum(np.abs(target - weights))
        weights = target
        rebalance_log.append({'Rebalance (first day with new weights)': full_dates[t].date(),
                              'N stocks': int(has_price.sum()), 'Turnover': turnover})
    # 3) portfolio return on day t and drift of the weights
    r_portfolio = np.sum(weights * R_full[t])
    weights = weights * (1 + R_full[t]) / (1 + r_portfolio)
    gross_returns.append(r_portfolio)
    daily_turnover.append(turnover)

group_full_gross = pd.Series(gross_returns, index=full_dates)
group_full_turnover = pd.Series(daily_turnover, index=full_dates)
group_full_net = group_full_gross - COST * group_full_turnover

rebalance_log = pd.DataFrame(rebalance_log)
print('Period:', full_dates[0].date(), 'to', full_dates[-1].date(), '|', len(full_dates), 'trading days |', len(rebalance_log), 'rebalancings')
print('First rebalancings:')
display(rebalance_log.head(3).round(4))
print(f"Average turnover per rebalancing (excluding the initial purchase): {rebalance_log['Turnover'].iloc[1:].mean():.3f}")

    GROUP: group_full_net,
    'SPY (total return)': returns.loc[full_dates, 'SPY'],

for name in full_series.columns:

    # Sterling (original definition): CAGR / (|average of the calendar-year maximum drawdowns| + 10%)
    # (17 calendar years; the last one, 2026, is year to date)
    yearly_mdd = []
    for year in years:
        in_year = full_dates.year == year
        yearly_mdd.append(compute_metrics(r[in_year], rf_full[in_year])['Max drawdown'])
    avg_yearly_mdd = np.mean(yearly_mdd)
    rows.append({
        'Portfolio': name,

        'Ann. volatility': m['Ann. volatility'],
        'Sharpe': m['Sharpe'],

        'Max drawdown': m['Max drawdown'],
        'Calmar': m['Calmar'],
        'Avg. calendar-year max drawdown': avg_yearly_mdd,
        'Sterling': m['Ann. return'] / (abs(avg_yearly_mdd) + 0.10),
        'Final value of 1 USD': (1 + r).prod(),
    })

13. Saving the results (CSV + Excel)¶

  • 04_experiment_design.csv — periods and stocks of each experiment (makes it possible to reproduce and reuse them in the individual project);
  • 04_metrics_by_experiment.csv — all the metrics, by experiment and portfolio (the 8 strategies, the Group pick and SPY);
  • 04_capm_by_experiment.csv — CAPM beta, Jensen's alpha, tracking error and information ratio against SPY, by experiment and portfolio (section 9.7);
  • 04_optimisation_failures.csv — every optimisation that failed twice (with ftol 1e-10 and then 1e-8); on those rebalancings we used equal weights; it may be empty;
  • 04_strategies_backtest.xlsx — all the summary tables, one per sheet (use this file to copy tables into the report), including the tables of the Group pick and of the head-to-head comparison (beats_group_pick, beats_spy, pairwise_*, universe23_*, fullsample_metrics, calendar_year_returns) and the CAPM medians (capm_median); each table is also saved as 04_<name>.csv.

14. Limitations (for the robustness section of the report)¶

  • Survivorship and selection bias (today's universe). The 23 stocks were chosen in September 2026 among today's largest companies. The brief allows today's universe if this is discussed ("discuss survivorship bias and any reliance on today's asset universe"). Consequences:
    • it inflates the absolute returns of every portfolio built from the 23 stocks (in the 12 years in which SPY fell, EW still earned ≈ +3.7% against ≈ −5.4% for SPY) and therefore every comparison with SPY;
    • it is not neutral between strategies: the five biggest winners of 2010-2026 (NVDA, AVGO, TSLA, MU, AMD) are also among the most volatile stocks. EW gives them 1/12 each, while inverse vol, ERC and GMV underweight them by design. So the hindsight flatters EW, Max decorrelation and Markowitz against the low-risk strategies. Without these five stocks (section 10.8) the return that ERC gives up against EW falls from ≈ 4.6 to ≈ 0.9 percentage points per year, and Markowitz loses its top return.
    • Drawing 12 of the 23 stocks at random does not remove the bias: all 23 are survivors.
  • The Group pick is EW on all 23 stocks. Against the 8 strategies (12 stocks each) its edge comes from holding 23 stocks instead of 12 (diversification), not from better stocks: on the same 23 stocks it is simply EW, and ERC and most diversified match it (section 11). Against SPY its advantage is the selection bias above, and its full-sample history (section 12) is not out-of-sample evidence.
  • Overlapping experiments (section 9.8): each out-of-sample day belongs to ≈ 7 experiments; at most 13 out-of-sample years do not overlap and they start in only 14 calendar years. The "% of experiments" are therefore much less precise than 100 independent tests would be: only the comparisons whose uncertainty band excludes 50% are treated as clear.
  • Few stress episodes: the sample starts in January 2010 (the first full year in which all the stocks except TSLA trade), so it excludes the 2008-09 financial crisis; the out-of-sample years (2012-2026) are mostly a rising market (only 12 experiments with SPY falling).
  • Estimation: 1-year historical means are very noisy (estimation error) — this mainly affects Markowitz and Max Sharpe.
  • Execution: the main convention trades at the close whose price is the last estimation input; a one-day lag (section 10.7) changes nothing material.
  • Simplified costs: fixed proportional cost, with no market impact and no taxes; SPY also has a management fee (~0.09%/year) that is already included in its price.
  • Drawdown ratios: with a single evaluation year, the Sterling ratio (|MDD| + 10%) is dominated by the 10% and ranks the portfolios almost like the return; Calmar is reported next to it (sections 7 and 9.2).
  • Risk-free rate: the 3-year Treasury carries some interest-rate risk; a 3-month T-bill would be the "purer" alternative. Its level lowers every Sharpe ratio by ≈ r_f / volatility (more for low-volatility portfolios) and enters the Max Sharpe optimisation.
  • Universe: only large-cap US stocks — the results may not apply to other asset classes.
