16. Conclusions and recommendation (guide for the report)¶

The numbers below come from this run (real FRED DGS3 series, extracted 8 October 2026); "≈" = rounded. Ten portfolios are compared: the 8 strategies of the brief, the Group pick (the group's 23 stocks in equal weights) and SPY. "Clear" means that the uncertainty band of section 9.8 (which accounts for the overlapping experiments) does not include 50%.

1. Among the 8 strategies of the brief, equally weighted (EW) is very hard to beat, and the top group cannot be separated. ERC (median Sharpe ≈ 1.80) and inverse vol (≈ 1.78) are level with EW (≈ 1.81); ERC beats EW in 51% of the experiments and inverse vol in 47%, and their uncertainty bands (≈ 36-68% and ≈ 30-67%) include 50% — EW, ERC, inverse vol and most diversified are statistically indistinguishable on the Sharpe ratio. By average rank in each experiment, ERC is the best of the 8 strategies in almost every variant (main ≈ 4.2 vs EW ≈ 4.5; new draw of stocks; all eligible stocks; one-day lag; years in which SPY fell; quarterly it is level with EW).

2. What is clear (bands far from 50%):

  • Markowitz, GMV and Max Sharpe lose to EW on the Sharpe ratio (Markowitz in 79% of the experiments, band ≈ 68-89%): this is estimation error — 1-year mean returns point to the recent winners. Markowitz is extremely concentrated (effective N ≈ 1.5, average maximum weight ≈ 77%), turns over ≈ 8 times more than EW and has a smaller drawdown than EW in only ≈ 9% of the experiments. A higher λ (5) reduces the risk but not the concentration (section 10.3).
  • The low-risk strategies reduce risk: ERC and inverse vol have lower volatility than EW in 100% of the experiments and smaller drawdowns in ≈ 86-87% (band ≈ 77-93%), with EW-like turnover (≈ 0.3 per year, ≈ 4 bps of cost); GMV has the lowest volatility (≈ 12.8%) but is concentrated (effective N ≈ 4.4) and has the lowest return.
  • ERC beats inverse vol (65% of the experiments, band ≈ 54-78%): taking correlations into account adds value.

3. Drawdown-based ratios. The low-risk strategies give up return: in the main universe ERC earns ≈ 4.6 percentage points less than EW in the same experiment. Per unit of drawdown they are therefore only level with EW (Calmar: ERC beats EW in 49% of the experiments) and behind it on the 1-year Sterling ratio (32%), which is dominated by the +10% in its denominator and ranks the portfolios almost like the return (section 7).

4. Part of that cost is hindsight (section 10.8). The five biggest winners of 2010-2026 are also very volatile, so EW (which holds them at 1/12) benefits from the way the universe was chosen more than ERC does. Without them, the return gap EW − ERC falls from ≈ 4.6 to ≈ 0.9 percentage points, ERC beats EW in 52% of the experiments, and Markowitz loses its top return (≈ 18% vs ≈ 22% for EW).

5. Against the index (SPY). Every portfolio built from the 23 stocks earns more than SPY in most experiments (ERC beats SPY on the Sharpe ratio in 86%, band ≈ 75-95%), but this is mostly the selection bias of today's universe and cannot be expected in real time. On risk, ERC is level with SPY in the main universe (lower volatility in only 46% of the experiments, smaller drawdown in 58%; both bands include 50%). Without the five biggest winners, ERC has lower volatility than SPY in 89% of the experiments and a smaller drawdown in 79%, with a higher Sharpe ratio in 83%. Its CAPM beta is ≈ 0.91 (section 9.7).

6. The Group pick (our 23 stocks in equal weights) has the best average rank (≈ 3.9 of 10) and wins the most head-to-head comparisons on the Sharpe ratio (68% on average). This edge comes from holding 23 stocks instead of 12 (diversification), not from better stocks: it beats EW (12 random stocks from the same 23) in 62% of the experiments (band ≈ 50-72%, at the limit), earns more than EW in only 49%, and on the same 23 stocks it is simply EW — ERC and most diversified match it (54% and 52%, section 11). Its edge over EW is smaller in 2021-2026 (56%) than in 2012-2016 (69%). Its 2010-2026 history (section 12) is descriptive only (hindsight).

7. Crashes. The drawdown protection of the low-risk strategies comes from moderate sell-offs (2018, 2022): in the 12 experiments in which SPY fell, ERC, inverse vol and GMV had a smaller drawdown than EW in 92% of them. In the March 2020 crash they fell as much as EW (e.g. experiment 62: ERC ≈ −31% vs EW ≈ −29%), because correlations rose towards 1.

8. Robustness of the implementation. Costs barely matter in this liquid universe (the average ranks move by less than 0.1 between 0 and 50 bps; Markowitz, the most expensive strategy, loses ≈ 33 bps per year at 10 bps). Quarterly rebalancing changes the Sharpe ratio of each strategy by at most ≈ 0.04 in the same experiment (median change) (the rank of the medians moves only because the medians sit close together). Trading one day later changes the medians by at most ≈ +0.07 (Markowitz) and the % beating EW by at most 2 percentage points.

9. Market risk (CAPM, section 9.7). Every portfolio has a positive median Jensen's alpha (≈ +6% to +18% per year), but it is significant in only ≈ 5-40% of the experiments and mostly reflects the selection bias. GMV is clearly defensive (β ≈ 0.64), ERC, inverse vol and most diversified have β ≈ 0.85-0.93, EW and the Group pick ≈ 1.04-1.05 and Markowitz ≈ 1.32.

Suggested recommendation (investor choosing between these strategies and the index)¶

  • Investor: a long-term investor in US large-cap equities who is choosing between buying the index (SPY) and running a rules-based portfolio of large US stocks, and who wants lower volatility and drawdowns without giving up risk-adjusted return, at low cost and low complexity.
  • Recommendation: risk parity (ERC) as the rules-based alternative. It is the most robust of the 8 strategies (best average rank in almost every variant; clearly better than inverse vol; volatility always below EW and drawdown below EW in ≈ 86% of the experiments; turnover ≈ 0.3 per year). Against the index, be honest about what the evidence shows: the higher returns of all 23-stock portfolios are mostly hindsight; what is left once the five biggest winners are removed is lower risk than SPY (volatility lower in ≈ 89% of the experiments, drawdown smaller in ≈ 79%) with a similar or higher Sharpe ratio. So the expected benefit is a smoother path at similar risk-adjusted return, not a higher return.
  • SPY remains the default for an investor who does not want to run a stock portfolio: it is cheaper, simpler and has no selection risk.
  • Not recommended: unconstrained Markowitz and Max Sharpe (extreme concentration, ≈ 8 times the turnover of EW, clearly worse than EW).
  • When to reconsider (measurable triggers): (i) ERC's realised volatility over the last 24 months is not below SPY's; (ii) a crash in which correlations jump (as in March 2020) — ERC gives no protection there; (iii) market leadership concentrated in a few high-volatility mega-caps, where ERC lags EW and the index; (iv) costs or turnover much higher than here (illiquid stocks); (v) weight limits or a shrinkage covariance (extensions A and B of the brief), which could make Markowitz and Max Sharpe usable; (vi) a universe defined by an ex-ante rule (e.g. the largest stocks of each sector at each date), which is the real test of the strategy without hindsight.
